analysis.one_liner: Extends Superfund's corporate and petroleum taxes for five years to fund toxic waste cleanup.
analysis.headline: The bill to extend Superfund's polluter-pays taxes for five years, with a collection ceiling of $22 billion, never left the Senate Finance Committee and died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have kept two "polluter pays" taxes alive for five more years: a tax on corporate income earmarked for the Superfund, and a per-barrel fee on petroleum. The money funds cleanup of the nation's worst toxic waste sites. The taxes had already expired at the end of 1995, and this bill would have revived and extended them through January 2001, raising the total that could be collected from about $12 billion to $22 billion.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in communities near hazardous waste sites, who benefit from continued federal funding for Superfund cleanups; the extension would have authorized $250 million per year in appropriations for fiscal years 1996 through 1999 and kept the trust fund's borrowing and spending authority alive. Taxpayers generally benefit too, because when the polluter-pays taxes lapse, cleanup costs shift onto the general Treasury.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the environmental income tax on corporations and the petroleum Superfund financing rate through January 1, 2001, instead of letting them expire as of January 1, 1996, keeping the polluter-pays funding stream for toxic site cleanup alive.
Raises the ceiling on Superfund taxes that may be collected from $11.97 billion to $22 billion and authorizes $250 million per year in appropriations to the fund for fiscal years 1996 through 1999.
Extends the deadline for repaying advances to the Superfund trust fund to December 31, 2000, keeping the fund's borrowing authority available for cleanup work.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, through the environmental income tax, and the petroleum industry, through the per-barrel Superfund fee; the petroleum fee is ordinarily passed along to consumers in the price of gasoline and oil products, so part of the cost lands on ordinary households at the pump.

drawbacks.text: The petroleum fee is an excise tax on oil products, which producers typically pass through to consumers, so part of the cleanup funding would be paid by households at the gasoline pump rather than by industry.

The bill's amendments to the trust fund's purposes are written by reference to the 'Superfund Reform Act of 1995,' citing that Act's CERCLA provisions 'as in effect on the date of the enactment' — but that broader reform bill was never enacted, so the cross-reference points to a statute that does not exist as drafted.

The corporate environmental tax is an income-based tax on corporations generally, not a fee tied to how much pollution a specific company created, so companies bear the cost regardless of their own contribution to contaminated sites.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On the merits, the bill is a modest, fairly conventional extension: it keeps a proven funding stream for toxic waste cleanup and shifts part of the cost from general taxpayers back to corporations and oil consumers. Its real problems are political and mechanical — it drew no cosponsors, arrived in the final weeks of a Congress that had already let the taxes lapse, and contains a drafting defect in that it depends on a 1995 reform act that never became law. As written it would likely have needed technical fixes before enactment.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Senator Frank Lautenberg introduced the bill on August 2, 1996, in the final months of the 104th Congress, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The bill attracted no cosponsors in the Senate.

The Superfund taxes the bill would have extended had already expired under existing law on January 1, 1996 — the bill's own text works by replacing 'January 1, 1996' deadlines with 'January 1, 2001' — so for the remainder of the Congress the polluter-pays funding stream stayed dormant.
No hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, and the bill received no further action before the Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations and the petroleum industry came out ahead, since the taxes stayed expired and no polluter-pays money was collected from them; communities near toxic sites and general taxpayers lost, because cleanup funding shifted away from polluter-pays sources.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporations that avoided the polluter-pays taxes

for.name: Sen. Frank Lautenberg
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend the Superfund taxes for five years and spoke on the Senate floor when introducing it.

against.name: Bob Packwood
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired never took up the bill; it received no hearing, markup, or vote after its referral.

against.name: Petroleum industry
against.role: Oil producers and refiners subject to the per-barrel Superfund fee
against.what_they_did: Opposed revival of the Superfund petroleum tax, which had expired at the end of 1995, and lobbied against its reinstatement during this period.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's only sponsor was a Democrat and it drew no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have reinstated the per-barrel Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate on petroleum through 2001, a fee the industry had escaped since it expired at the end of 1995. Much of the fee is passed to consumers in fuel prices, so the industry's interest in keeping it expired ran against dedicated cleanup funding.

The bill extends the corporate environmental income tax, a tax on corporate income earmarked for Superfund, for five more years. With the tax expired, corporations paid nothing toward hazardous site cleanup from this source; the bill would have put them back on the hook.

industries.industry: Hazardous waste cleanup and remediation contractors
industries.note: Continued Superfund appropriations of $250 million per year would have funded site remediation work performed by environmental engineering and cleanup firms. Letting the bill die kept that revenue stream uncertain, alongside the communities waiting for cleanups.
